implementation_notes: C has no exception mechanism at all, which makes this the clearest case in the catalogue: the only way to write programming by exception in C is `setjmp`/`longjmp`, and Wilson's locality argument is written precisely about C — absent `longjmp`, `fork` and `exit`, it is possible to look at a sample of C code and understand its flow and, within the limits of the abstraction, its semantics. `longjmp` restores the stack pointer and program counter and skips every cleanup in between, so a stack-allocated lock or buffer is left held; using it for anything other than a whole-process abort is unsound, not merely poor style. The correct C form is `errno` plus a return-code check at every call, or a struct return with a status field.
idiom_name: setjmp/longjmp used as a break; errno as an implicit channel
alternative: Return an error code (or set `errno`) from the function and branch on it; use a tagged struct or an out-parameter where the failure carries data; use `goto` to a single cleanup label at the end of the function for early exit, which is the structured C idiom rather than a nonlocal jump.
pitfalls: `longjmp` out of a frame holding a mutex or an allocated buffer is a memory and locking bug, not only a readability one.
`errno` is only meaningful immediately after a documented failing call, which requires discipline that `longjmp` neatly bypasses.
`goto fail;` at the bottom of a function is the structured alternative and is not programming by exception — the distinction is a single forward jump to a cleanup label, not a nonlocal unwind.
